study.title: Psalm 7 - Call for God's righteousness and end in praise
study.overview: This psalm presents David amid accusations and persecution, seeking refuge in the Lord and appealing to divine justice. He begins with an urgent request for deliverance, goes through a solemn affirmation of innocence, calls for God to intervene as a judge, and ends with confidence that God himself will do justice. The main movement of the text is from the lament to worship: anguish is not denied, but it is placed before a God who examines hearts, sustains the righteous and judges the wicked.

outline.title: Clamor by deliverance before stalkers
outline.explanation: David addresses the Lord with personal confidence and asks for the ransom of those who hunt him. The image of the lion highlights the violence and urgency of the threat, suggesting real and overwhelming danger.

outline.title: Declaration of innocence and handing over the case to God
outline.explanation: He takes a conditional oath: if he has acted wickedly, he accepts to suffer the consequence. This is not empty self-defense, but a surrender of his case to God's righteous judgment.

outline.title: Call for God to rise as a judge
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks that God intervene publicly, judge the peoples and firm the righteous. Here arises divine justice, the examination of hearts, and the confidence that God is the shield of the upright.

outline.title: Judgment against the wicked and conclusion in praise
outline.explanation: The psalm states that God is a just judge and that evil returns over who practices it. The end is a confession of worship: David praises the Lord for his righteousness and his exalted name.

study.context: The title informs that this is a song of David connected to the words of Kuxe, a descendant of Benjamin. The given notes understand Cuxe as someone hostile to David, possibly a relative of Saul or Saul himself indirectly mentioned. The immediate context is of unjust accusations and persecution, which explains the tone of defense, supplication and confidence in the verdict of God.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that the righteousness of God is not abstract: he observes, judges, and acts in history. David's prayer combines humility and firmness; he does not deny the divine examination, but invites him to take place. The innocence claimed in the text is not an affirmation of sinless perfection, but of integrity as to specific accusations. The Lord appears as an impartial judge, shield of the correct heart and sovereign who makes evil return on the evildoer. There is also a theology of moral reversal: the violence planned by the ungodly turns against himself, and the trust of the righteous culminates in praise. In evangelical Christian reading, the pattern of the unjustly afflicted righteous points to a Messianic echo, but the first sense of the psalm remains as a prayer of a sufferer who trusts in divine righteousness.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm ends in praise because, in the lamentations of Psalms 3 to 7, the normal way is to move from the complaint to worship; the name "High" emphasizes that God is just and trustworthy, and his command prevails.

David presents his cause to God and, by faith, awaits the divine verdict against his persecutors; the confidence in the end of the psalm is that God will do justice and return evil upon the head of the wicked.
The expression "if I do not repent" is seen as linked to the sequence of verses about the just judge: God angers against sin and already prepares his judgment against the unrepentant.

questions: When I am accused or misunderstood, do I take my case first to God or just try to defend myself?
Is my conscience before the Lord so sincere that I can humbly ask him to examine my motivations?
Have I learned to turn distress into trust and praise, as David does at the end of the psalm?
study.practice: Pray honestly when suffering injustice: present the facts to God without exaggeration, without vengeance and without despair. Examine your own life before the Lord, asking him to reveal hidden motives. If you are wronged, choose to answer with prayer, integrity, and patience, trusting that God judges with righteousness at the right time. Finish your prayer by remembering who God is: righteous, strong and worthy of praise.
study.uncertainty: The title of the psalm mentions Cuxe, but the notes provided do not allow them to identify with certainty that person. Nor is it possible to affirm, based only on the material given, all the historical details behind the accusation against David. Messianic reading is a possible Christian application, but it is not the direct meaning explained in the notes.
